fieldMarks: Large, stocky, marbled gold and brown salamander with a rounded, wide wedge-shaped head, fleshy legs and a laterally compressed tail (WDFW; BC).
Largest terrestrial salamander in North America: to about 6.7 in snout-vent and 13.4 in total length; marbling may persist only on the head of very old animals (WDFW).
12-13 costal grooves, indistinct; underside white to light gray, unmarked (WDFW).
Larvae are stream-type: short gills, low tail fin ending near the hind limbs, hard black digit tips (WDFW).
behavior: Larvae are active on the streambed at night and under cover by day (NatureServe).
Adults eat terrestrial invertebrates, small snakes, shrews, mice and other salamanders; larvae eat aquatic invertebrates and some small vertebrates (NatureServe).
Migrates between aquatic breeding and terrestrial non-breeding habitat; larvae usually metamorphose in 18-24 months, some become sexually mature as larvae (NatureServe).
Female attends eggs laid in water-filled chambers under rocks or logs in or beside streams (NatureServe; BC).
habitat: Small to medium mountain streams in moist coniferous forest; larvae in clear, cold, well-oxygenated streams under stones; transformed adults in humid forest under rocks and logs near streams (WDFW; NatureServe).
range: Extreme southwestern British Columbia (Chilliwack River drainage) south through western Washington and Oregon to northwestern California (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Cope's giant salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: Pacific giant is larger with a wider head and longer legs; when legs are pressed against the body the toes touch or cross (WDFW).

lookalikes.name: Torrent salamanders (Rhyacotriton)
lookalikes.howToTell: Stream larvae have orange undersides and tiny gills barely visible out of water (WDFW).
